name: Table 'No. 16' designed by Carl Hörvik
description: Table Model 16 was designed by Carl Hörvik for use in offices and waiting rooms, combining a circular stone top with a restrained metal frame. The substantial top rests within a shallow perimeter rim, while four flat-section legs are joined by a geometric cross-shaped support below. The design reflects Hörvik’s early functionalist approach, in which material and structure take precedence over applied decoration. Its compact proportions and durable construction made it particularly suited to public and institutional interiors, while the simplicity of the frame anticipates the more industrial language that would later become central to Scandinavian modern furniture. Carl Hörvik was a Swedish architect and designer associated with the transition from Swedish Grace to functionalism. A contemporary of Gunnar Asplund, he worked across architecture, interiors and furniture, producing designs for both domestic and public environments. His work is characterised by strong proportions, practical materials and a direct expression of construction.

name: Desk designed by a Danish Cabinetmaker
description: This Danish cabinetmaker’s desk was made in the 1930s from root wood and nutwood. The front is arranged with five drawers, set within a rectilinear frame and raised on straight legs. The design is restrained in form, allowing the material and quality of the veneer work to define the character of the piece. The drawer fronts are veneered in richly figured root wood, with bookmatched panels that create a symmetrical movement across the surface. Root wood was a highly valued material during this period, often used for furniture intended for refined domestic interiors. In this example, the cabinetmaker has used the veneer not simply as surface covering, but as the main expressive element of the design. The desk reflects the transition in Danish furniture during the 1930s, when traditional cabinetmaking techniques were increasingly combined with cleaner geometric forms. Its rounded drawer edges, recessed working space and balanced proportions connect it to early European Art Deco and Functionalism, while the careful use of figured wood maintains a strong link to classical craftsmanship.

name: Pair of bedside tables 'Model 914' designed by Josef Frank for Svenskt Tenn
description: Model 914 is a refined bedside table designed by Josef Frank in the 1950s for Svenskt Tenn. Executed in mahogany, the design is defined by its clear proportions: a rectangular top with raised edges, a single drawer fitted with a curved brass handle, and an open shelf below for additional storage. Josef Frank created approximately 2,000 designs for Svenskt Tenn, shaping the company’s identity through furniture that balances function, craftsmanship and a humanistic approach to modern living. Model 914 forms part of this enduring body of work.

name: Hall bench for DUX
description: This hall bench produced by DUX in Sweden, combines a rattan frame with a teak top and an open slatted shelf below. The gently curved supports, wrapped joints and raised border around the top give the piece a light, crafted character, while the lower shelf provides practical storage for shoes or smaller objects. The design reflects the Scandinavian interest in natural materials combined with influences from colonial furniture. DUX was originally established as a manufacturer of beds and later expanded its production to include furniture by leading Swedish designers, most notably Bruno Mathsson.

name: Pair of bedside tables 'Model 36' designed by Severin Hansen Jr. for Illums Bolighus
description: These 'Model 36' bedside tables by Severin Hansen Jr. for Illums Bolighus is a refined example of Danish modern design. Executed in richly figured rosewood, each table displays the dramatic grain and warm depth that made the timber especially prized in Scandinavian furniture of the period. A defining feature of the design is the precise three-way mitred joinery at the corners, a hallmark closely associated with Hansen’s work. This technically demanding construction allows the grain to flow cleanly around the edges, creating a seamless form. Stamped

name: Side table designed by Sten Blomberg for David Blomberg AB
description: This side table was designed by Sten Blomberg for David Blomberg AB in Sweden in 1933. Executed in black-painted birch with a nickel-plated top and fittings, it reflects the shift in Swedish furniture design during the early 1930s, when the refinement of Swedish Grace began to give way to the more rational language of functionalism. The construction is deliberately restrained, with a rectilinear body, one drawer and an open shelf below. The black surface gives the table a strong architectural presence, while the metal-lined top introduces a practical and slightly industrial element. Sten Blomberg worked for David Blomberg AB between 1932 and 1937, during a period when Swedish interiors were moving towards cleaner forms and more functional solutions. The company was founded by his father, David Blomberg, an important figure in Swedish design history and the first artistic director and head of the furniture department at Nordiska Kompaniet.

name: Sewing table designed by Josef Frank for Svenskt Tenn
description: This sewing table was designed by Josef Frank for Svenskt Tenn in Sweden during the mid-twentieth century. Veneered in walnut and fitted with brass details, it combines practical storage with the light, domestic character that defines much of Frank’s furniture. The table is arranged in two tiers, with drawers set into both levels and a suspended curved compartment below for yarn or sewing materials. One drawer is fitted with internal compartments, reflecting the object’s original function as a working piece of furniture. The castors allow it to be moved easily within an interior, while the stepped construction gives the table an open and architectural quality. Born in Austria, Josef Frank trained as an architect in Vienna before moving to Sweden, where he began working with Svenskt Tenn in 1934. His furniture and textile designs became central to the company’s identity for several decades, offering an alternative to stricter functionalism through warmth, comfort and adaptability.

name: Occasional table ‘Annika’ designed by Bruno Mathsson for Karl Mathsson
description: The "Annika" table, designed by Swedish architect and furniture designer Bruno Mathsson, exemplifies his commitment to functionalism and modernism. Introduced in the 1930s, this table showcases Mathsson's innovative use of materials and his dedication to ergonomic design. Mathsson's practice of naming his furniture designs after women, such as the "Annika" table, was a distinctive feature of his work. However, specific details about the origins of these names, including whether they were inspired by individuals he knew personally, are not well-documented Bruno Mathsson, born in 1907 in Värnamo, Sweden, was deeply influenced by his family's legacy of master cabinetmaking. His design philosophy harmoniously blended traditional Swedish craftsmanship with the principles of modernism. Throughout his career, Mathsson developed innovative techniques for bending wood and explored ergonomic designs, leading to iconic furniture pieces that remain highly regarded in the design community. Stamped

name: Occasional table 'Model AT-10' designed by Hans J Wegner for Andreas Tuck
description: The AT-10 occasional table, designed by Hans J. Wegner for Andreas Tuck in the 1950s, exemplifies Wegner's ability to combine functionality with simple, elegant design. Crafted from teak and oak, the table features a finely crafted solid wood top and a woven cane shelf below, showcasing Wegner’s attention to detail and his mastery of materials. Hans J. Wegner, often referred to as the father of Danish design, revolutionized mid-century furniture through his innovative approach to form and material. Growing up as the son of a cobbler, Wegner developed a profound appreciation for craftsmanship and a deep understanding of wood’s potential. Over his lifetime, he created more than 500 designs, many of which have become icons of modern design. His philosophy was rooted in creating furniture that was simple, genuine, and alive with the spirit of the material. This occasional table reflects those ideals, with its clean lines and thoughtful construction. The woven cane shelf adds both functionality and a sense of lightness, making it suitable for various interiors. Wegner’s designs have had a lasting impact, and pieces like the AT-10 continue to embody the timeless qualities that have brought Danish furniture to international acclaim.

name: Side table model 6 designed by Helge Vestergaard Jensen manufactured by Jason Møbler
description: Side table 'Model 6' in rosewood produced by Jason Møbler demonstrates Helge Vestergaard Jensen’s disciplined approach to proportion and material. The compact form is elevated by subtly rounded edges, a softly framed apron and legs that taper with precision. The single drawer is discreetly integrated, fitted with small brass pulls that provide a restrained contrast to the depth of the rosewood. Produced by Jason Møbler in the 1960s, a manufacturer associated with high standards of cabinetmaking, the table reflects the collaborative excellence that helped define Danish modern furniture internationally. Jensen was recognised for his exacting craftsmanship and he is frequently described as one of the more sculptural figures among the Danish modern masters. Although Jensen’s output was relatively limited, this makes his pieces today highly collectible, valued for their refined detailing and material integrity.

name: Sideboard
description: This timeless sideboard veneered in richly grained elm and dating from the 1930s-1940s reflects the careful craftsmanship and balanced proportions characteristic of Scandinavian furniture from the mid-century. Two drawers integrated into the apron provide storage, while the cabinet below offers a generous interior. Pieces like this emerged during a transitional moment in Nordic furniture design, when traditional woodworking techniques were still central, yet forms were becoming more restrained and attuned.

name: Coffee table 'Annika' designed by Bruno Mathsson for Firma Karl Mathsson
description: This table is notable for its use of solid birch and its low, elongated proportions, characteristic of Bruno Mathsson’s work with lightweight wooden furniture during the mid-20th century. Bruno Mathsson (1907–1988) was active as a designer and architect in Sweden from the 1930s onward and is known for his systematic exploration of wood, particularly birch. Trained as a cabinetmaker in Värnamo, he developed furniture based on studies of sitting and resting positions, often combining bentwood techniques with restrained structural solutions. The "Annika" series belongs to a group of designs from the post-war period in which Mathsson focused on simple domestic furniture intended for flexible use in modern interiors. Alongside seating such as the Eva and Pernilla chairs, low tables and benches formed part of this wider body of work. The table has a long, rectangular top with softly rounded corners, supported by gently curved legs set close to the ends and centre. The legs are shaped from solid birch, tapering toward the floor and joined directly to the underside of the top. The construction is minimal, with no cross-bracing, relying on the strength of the wood and the leg geometry for stability. The height and proportions allow the piece to function either as a bench or as a low table. Stamped Bruno Mathsson Design & Firma Karl Mathsson

name: Coffee table designed by Bernt Petersen for Henrik Wørts
description: This rectangular coffee table by Bernt Petersen was produced in Denmark in the 1950s–60s for the joinery workshop of Henrik Wørts. The table is notable for its use of rosewood and for the distinctive leg design, in which the gently tapering supports end in small "crochet hooks" at the feet, a characteristic feature of this model. Bernt Petersen (1937–2017) trained as a cabinetmaker and studied at the Denmark Design School, graduating in 1960. He worked with Mobilia and with Hans J. Wegner before establishing his own practice in 1963, and later taught at the Denmark Design School and the Royal Danish Academy’s Furniture School. Petersen’s work from the mid-20th century includes furniture in light hardwoods and occasional pieces in rosewood, designed with attention to proportion, material, and joinery. Many of his tables and other designs were made by specialist cabinetmakers in Denmark, including Wørts Møbelsnedkeri. The table has a long, slim tabletop in richly figured rosewood with clean edges and sharp, mitred corners. The surface grain runs lengthwise, emphasising the wood’s linear pattern. The legs are also in rosewood, gently tapering as they descend and ending in subtle hooked details at their base. The joinery is precise and the surfaces are hand-finished, resulting in a table with clear lines and an overall balanced proportion.

name: Desk 'RY 32' designed by Hans J Wegner for Ry Møbler.
description: This oak desk, model RY 32, was designed by Hans J. Wegner and produced in Denmark by Ry Møbler in the 1950s. It is characterised by a straightforward rectangular top supported on tapered legs, and a single front drawer featuring circular wooden handles and a small keyhole. The desk’s proportions and simple detailing reflect its intended function as a writing surface for a home or study. The RY 32 belongs to a period in Wegner’s career when he was extending his work beyond seating into other types of furniture, applying the same attention to proportion and joinery in tables and desks. Wegner trained as a cabinetmaker before studying at the Denmark Design School, and throughout his career he maintained a focus on wood as a primary material, favouring joinery that made structural elements durable. This desk was part of his collaboration with Ry Møbler, whose workshops executed his designs using traditional techniques.

name: Magazine table designed by Bruno Mathsson  for Firma Karl Mathsson
description: This magazine table by Bruno Mathsson, produced by Firma Karl Mathsson in Värnamo and designed in 1964, is notable for combining a low table with integrated magazine storage in a single structure. The table belongs to a period in Mathsson’s career when he focused on lightweight wooden constructions and furniture intended for everyday use. During the 1960s, his work for the family firm in Värnamo often explored how bent laminated wood could be used to create stable yet visually reduced forms. This table reflects that approach, bringing together structural clarity and practical function without additional decorative elements. The tabletop is made from masur birch with softly rounded corners and rests on bent laminated birch legs that lift the surface slightly from the floor. Set into one side of the top are four recessed openings holding white lacquered metal magazine compartments. The table is marked Firma Karl Mathsson, confirming its production by the Mathsson workshop in Sweden.

name: Dining table model '91' designed by Alvar Aalto O.Y. Huonekalu-ja Rakennustyötehdas A.B, for Finmar Ltd,
description: This round birch dining table by Alvar Aalto for Artek is an elegant example of early Finnish modern design. Classified as model A 91, it is accompanied by its original removable rotating serving tray, the “Lazy Susan” model B 91, which can be placed on the tabletop when in use or stored separately. The broad circular top rests on three characteristically Aalto legs in bent laminated birch, whose gentle curve softens the otherwise rigorously functional form. Conceived in the mid-1930s and exhibited at the Milan Triennale in 1936, the table reflects Aalto’s interest in democratic, practical furniture for modern living. The legs can be dismantled with ease, a feature deliberately developed at Artek to simplify shipping and storage for international clients. Warmly patinated birch highlights the natural grain of the wood, giving the modernist structure a tactile, organic presence. As a historic Alvar Aalto table complete with its B 91 serving tray, this piece embodies the blend of innovation, craftsmanship and understated refinement that defines Nordic design.

name: Dining table Superellipse designed by Bruno Mathsson & Piet Hein
description: The Superellipse table was designed by Bruno Mathsson in collaboration with Piet Hein in the 1960s. This dining table is based on the superellipse, a geometric curve named and popularised by Piet Hein in the late 1950s. The form combines properties of the rectangle and the ellipse, resulting in an elongated surface with rounded ends and no sharp corners. Hein first applied the superellipse to urban planning, notably in a traffic design proposal for Sergels Torg, before adapting the form to domestic objects. The tabletop follows this superelliptical outline and is in rosewood. The edge profile is thin and gently rounded, giving the top a light visual appearance while maintaining structural rigidity. The surface is plain and unornamented. The table stands on four slender chromed steel legs, slightly splayed to provide stability while minimising visual weight. Produced in several sizes and finishes, the Superellipse table exemplifies the integration of mathematical geometry into functional furniture design characteristic of post-war Scandinavian modernism.

name: Three rosewood nesting tables model  41A and 41B. designed by Severin Hansen Jr
description: Nesting tables models 41A and 41B, designed by Severin Hansen and produced by Haslev Møbelsnedkeri, Denmark, 1950s, are executed in rosewood and conceived as a coherent set of one larger table with two smaller tables that slide neatly beneath. The construction is characteristic of Hansen’s work, where precise joinery define the structure. The legs meet the aprons in clean, angular transitions, and the proportions are carefully calibrated so that each table functions independently while remaining consistent as part of the set. The nesting format reflects the practical thinking of Danish mid-century interiors. Severin Hansen collaborated closely with Haslev Møbelfabrik throughout the post-war period, producing small-scale furniture in teak and rosewood. His nesting tables, desks and side tables are now recognised for their refined construction and understated elegance, representing a restrained but highly resolved expression of Danish mid century design.

name: Dining table designed by Mogens Kold
description: This dining table was produced in Denmark in the 1960s by Mogens Kold, a furniture manufacturer. The rectangular top incorporates an extension mechanism that allows the table to be enlarged for additional seating. When closed, the tabletop presents a clean, uninterrupted surface. The corners are softly rounded and the edge is subtly profiled, giving the top a thin visual appearance while maintaining structural stability. The legs are slender, tapered, and slightly angled, with no decorative detailing. The construction prioritises clarity, precision, and functional efficiency. Mogens Kold was known primarily as a high-quality manufacturer rather than as an individual designer. The firm produced furniture aligned with Danish modern principles, combining functional solutions, careful joinery, and restrained proportions intended for everyday use. Marked.

name: A pair of occasional tables 'Oktober' designed by Carl Malmsten
description: The “Oktober” occasional tables were designed by Malmsten as compact, versatile furnishings suitable for informal domestic use. Their proportions were intended to accommodate tea service, reading light or lamp placement during the autumn months—hence the name “Oktober”, chosen to reflect the seasonal gathering indoors. Executed in warm‑toned hardwood with clean lines and modest detailing, the tables display Malmsten’s commitment to craftsmanship and to a human‑centred approach to furniture design. The design retains a sense of simplicity while offering practical mobility and flexibility. Design context Carl Malmsten’s work is rooted in Swedish craft tradition and he was critical of the austerity of functionalism. The “Oktober” table series reflects his philosophy of furniture as a part of everyday life—furniture designed for presence rather than spectacle. The surfaces show natural signs of age and use, consistent with well-preserved examples from the period. Joints, veneers, and top finishes retain the clarity of their original construction while reflecting the passage of time through subtle shifts in tone and patina.

name: Tray table designed by Rut Bryk for Arabia
description: Between 1944 and 1947, Rut Bryk created a limited series of trays for Arabia, featuring motifs that ranged from still lifes to depictions of life events such as funerals and, as in this case, weddings. Interestingly, Rut Bryk married Tapio Wirkkala in 1945 — just one year before the tray in question was made. These trays were included in several exhibitions during the mid-1940s, among them a notable showing at Nordiska Kompaniet in 1945. Writing about that exhibition in the magazine Form, Åke Stavenow remarked that Bryk had brought her artistic expression to such a level of refinement that further development along the same path seemed almost inconceivable. Rut Bryk (1916–1999) was a pioneering Finnish ceramic artist and designer renowned for her innovative contributions to modern ceramic art. Born in Stockholm, she studied graphic design in Helsinki before joining the Arabia ceramics factory in 1942. Throughout her career, Bryk received numerous accolades, such as the Grand Prix at the 1951 Milan Triennial and the Pro Finlandia medal in 1962.

name: Occasional table model 2126 designed by Josef Frank for Svenskt Tenn
description: Josef Frank's Table 2126, designed in 1951 for Svenskt Tenn, reflects his signature blend of function and character. The small table features a round elm burl veneer top—with its unique pattern—supported by a mahogany base. The model is originally part of the furnishings in Josef and Anna Frank’s Stockholm apartment, the model was later included in the 1968 memorial exhibition at the National Museum. Josef Frank (1885–1967) was an Austrian-Swedish architect and designer who became a leading voice in 20th-century Scandinavian design. After relocating to Sweden in the 1930s, he began a lasting collaboration with Svenskt Tenn, producing furniture, textiles, and lighting that continue to define a uniquely humanistic and enduring design legacy.

name: Trolley model 901 designed by Alvar Aalto
description: Alvar Aalto designed the Tea Trolley 901 in 1936, during a highly productive period that included his architectural work for the Finnish Pavilion at the 1937 Paris World’s Fair. The trolley reflects his broader interest in creating a complete visual and spatial language for interiors — furniture that complemented his architecture both functionally and emotionally. He drew inspiration from British tea culture and Japanese woodwork, particularly the idea of hospitality as an aesthetic and moral value. The 901 trolley is built from birch wood, one of Aalto’s preferred materials for its lightness and pliability. The frame features his signature bentwood technique, creating smooth, continuous curves that give the trolley its sculptural elegance and visual softness. These trolleys are now considered icons of Scandinavian modernism — collected by design institutions like MoMA and the Vitra Design Museum, and still used in both homes and public spaces. Alvar Aalto (1898–1976) was a Finnish architect and designer known for his humanistic approach to modernism. A pioneer of Scandinavian design, he blended function with warmth, using natural materials, soft curves, and organic forms in both buildings and furniture. He once said, “You can’t build a house for a man without understanding him.” That humanism extended to his designs — he believed sharp angles felt aggressive and unwelcoming. That’s why so many of his buildings and furniture pieces flow with soft, organic curves — he wanted his architecture to “greet the body like a handshake.”

name: Desk designed by Tove Kindt-Larsen and Edvard Kindt-Larsen for Thorald Madsen. H.
description: This freestanding desk by Tove and Edvard Kindt-Larsen is distinguished by the subtle shaping of the tabletop, where the edges rise slightly to form a shallow surround. Produced by cabinetmaker Thorald Madsen, the piece reflects a careful balance between utility and proportion typical of their work from the mid 20th century. Tove and Edvard Kindt-Larsen were a pioneering Danish design duo whose collaborative work significantly influenced mid century Scandinavian design. Both trained under the esteemed Kaare Klint at the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts where they combined architectural principles with a deep understanding of materials to create furniture, textiles, silverware, and lighting that embodied the essence of Danish Modernism.

name: Serving trolley model 2248 designed by Josef Frank for Svenskt Tenn
description: Josef Frank designed several serving trolleys throughout his career at Svenskt Tenn. This model, 2248 reflects his signature approach to furniture: functional, yet full of personality, with organic lines, playful proportions. It has four castors, making it easy to move—underscoring its purpose as both a mobile service piece and a versatile furnishing. Josef Frank (1885–1967) was an Austrian-born architect and designer who became a central figure in Swedish modern design. After moving from Austria to Sweden in the 1930s, he became a defining force at Svenskt Tenn. Frank believed that design should enhance everyday life—not impose on it—leading to creations that are as joyful as they are functional. His work remains a cornerstone of Scandinavian design, celebrated for its warmth, originality, and timeless appeal.

name: Dining table 'Pyramid' designed by Carl Malmsten for J.O Carlsson
description: The Pyramid dining table was designed by Carl Malmsten in the early 1940s and produced in Sweden by J.O. Carlsson. It is an extendable dining table composed of a circular top with two removable extension leaves, allowing the table to expand into an elongated oval format. The circular tabletop is veneered. The perimeter is finished with a continuous inlaid band of stylised ornamental motifs in contrasting woods. Produced by J.O. Carlsson, a manufacturer known for workshop-based production and high-quality cabinetmaking, the table reflects Malmsten’s emphasis on durable construction, precise woodworking, and carefully considered surface treatment in domestic furniture of the period.

name: 'Schroeder' occasional table designed by Gerrit Rietveld
description: The ‘Schroeder’ side table is an excellent example of the bold geometry and visionary design of the De Stijl movement. Produced by G.A. van de Groenekan, the table features an eye-catching composition of primary colours paired with clean, angular lines. These principles were central to the De Stijl movement which was based upon strict ideals of vertical and horizontal geometry. Much like Nordic design, the ‘Schroeder’ table is a harmonious blend of art and functionality. The asymmetrical structure challenged conventional design norms while remaining practical for modern living. Rietveld believed in creating furniture that challenged conventional aesthetics and hierarchy. The Schroeder Table’s asymmetrical design exemplifies this. It doesn’t conform to traditional ideas of balance but instead explores new spatial relationships. The bold use of red, black, and white—the hallmark palette of De Stijl—demonstrates how art can be translated into everyday objects. The table takes its name from Truus Schröder, Rietveld’s close collaborator and patron. Schröder commissioned Rietveld to design her iconic home, the Rietveld Schröder House, which is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The table reflects the same dynamic interplay of planes, colours, and functionality seen in the house. It was conceived as part of a vision where furniture and architecture worked together to create a seamless, modern living environment.

name: Pair of bedside tables for DUX
description: The colonial-style combination of cane, rattan, and teak makes this Scandinavian bedside table design particularly interesting. The woven edges and metal handles create a striking decorative contrast. Both bedside tables are very sturdy and in good original condition. Initially, the Swedish furniture manufacturer DUX specialised in the production of beds, but later they diversified and famously realised various iconic designs by Bruno Mathsson.

name: Desk model JH571 designed by Hans J. Wegner for Johannes Hansen
description: The Architect’s Desk, model JH571, was designed by Hans J. Wegner for the Copenhagen cabinetmaker Johannes Hansen in 1953 and first presented in 1954 at the Copenhagen Cabinetmakers’ Guild Exhibition. The desk belongs to the post-war period of Danish furniture design and is among the relatively few desks designed by Wegner. The desk features a solid teak tabletop, oak legs set at an angle, and metal stretchers holding those legs in place. The two drawers are suspended from the underside of the tabletop rather than integrated into the structure, leaving the construction visually open and giving the desk a restrained, architectural expression that reflects the “Architect’s Desk” name. Produced in limited numbers by Johannes Hansen, the JH571 desk is characteristic of the cabinetmaker’s work in the early 1950s.

name: Dining table
description: This Swedish Modern dining table from the 1930s/40s embodies the elegant simplicity and craftsmanship characteristic of the period. Constructed with a sturdy oak frame, the table features gently tapering legs that lend a refined, sculptural quality. The most striking element is the playful scalloped apron along the table’s edge. The clean lines and restrained detailing reflect the principles of Swedish Modernism, where functionality meets artistry. Despite being of anonymous design, the table exemplifies the period's emphasis on quality craftsmanship and timeless elegance, making it a unique and versatile piece for both modern and traditional interiors.

name: Bench/coffee table “Annika” designed by Bruno Mathsson for Karl Mathsson
description: As one of Sweden's most celebrated designers, Bruno Mathsson was renowned for his innovative use of wood. Seen in the gently curved legs, made out of solid birch, is Mathsson’s skill in woodworking and his ability to shape the wood. The "Annika" bench exemplifies his approach to design—where simplicity, natural materials, and craftsmanship come together to create timeless, functional pieces. Designed to serve both as a bench and coffee table, the "Annika" is versatile and adaptable to various interiors. Its light proportions and clean lines make it suitable for modern and traditional spaces alike. Bruno Mathsson (1907–1988) was a leading Swedish designer and architect renowned for his pioneering work in Scandinavian modernism. Known for his mastery of wood bending techniques, Mathsson created furniture that combined functionality, comfort, and elegance. His iconic works, such as the Eva, Pernilla, and Annika chairs and tables, feature organic forms and light, sculptural silhouettes. Mathsson’s use of natural materials like birch and elm showcased his deep respect for craftsmanship and the beauty of simplicity. His timeless designs remain celebrated for their innovation and enduring appeal.

name: Coffee table
description: This mid-century coffee table, crafted by an anonymous Danish designer, highlights the simplicity and utility characteristic of Scandinavian design from the 1950s and 1960s. Produced in Denmark during a golden age of design innovation, this piece seamlessly blends functionality with understated elegance. A standout feature is the discreet single drawer beneath the tabletop, providing practical storage for small items while maintaining the table's sleek profile. The gently rounded corners and elegantly tapered legs reflect the craftsmanship and minimalist aesthetic.

name: Set of four nesting tables designed by Aksel Kjersgaard
description: This set of four nesting tables, designed by Aksel Kjersgaard in Denmark during the 1960s, exemplifies the refined simplicity of Danish Modern design. Crafted from Brazilian rosewood, the tables feature clean lines and a minimalist rectangular form. Aksel Kjersgaard was celebrated for his focus on precision craftsmanship and his ability to balance form and function seamlessly. His designs often embraced the natural character of wood, creating pieces that are both understated and elegant. This set of tables is a testament to his approach, embodying timeless design principles that make them as relevant today as they were in the mid-20th century.

name: Desk, designed by Helge Sibast for Sibast Furniture
description: This executive desk, designed by Helge Sibast exemplifies Danish modern design with its clean lines, refined craftsmanship, and functional elegance. Featuring ample storage, refined brass details, and clean architectural lines, it serves as both a practical workspace and a statement piece. Ideal for a contemporary office, study, or collector’s space, this desk showcases the enduring appeal of Danish Modern design, where form and function come together seamlessly. Helge Sibast (1908–1985) was a Danish furniture designer and cabinetmaker, celebrated for his contributions to Danish Modern design during the mid-20th century. Sibast was part of Denmark’s golden era of design. His work is distinguished by its exceptional craftsmanship, clean lines, and innovative use of wood, hallmarks of Danish furniture design. Helge Sibast grew up immersed in woodworking; he trained as a cabinetmaker under his father and eventually took over the family business. His deep respect for traditional woodworking techniques is evident in his designs.

name: Dining table designed by Arne Vodder for Sibast
description: This rosewood dining table features a seamlessly integrated extendable design, allowing for effortless expansion to accommodate larger gatherings without compromising its elegant profile. Precision joinery and expert craftsmanship are evident in the table’s solid frame and smooth extension mechanism, ensuring stability and ease of use. The slender, tapered legs, provide both strength and a visually light footprint, contributing to the table’s refined silhouette. Subtle decoration is added by the rosewood figuring in the table’s surface.

name: Dining table designed by Arne Vodder for Sibast,
description: This rosewood dining table features a seamlessly integrated extendable design, allowing for effortless expansion to accommodate larger gatherings without compromising its elegant profile. Precision joinery and expert craftsmanship are evident in the table’s solid frame and smooth extension mechanism, ensuring stability and ease of use. The slender, tapered legs, provide both strength and a visually light footprint, contributing to the table’s refined silhouette. Subtle decoration is added by the rosewood figuring in the table’s surface.

name: Bench/coffee table “Annika” designed by Bruno Mathsson for Karl Mathsson,
description: A refined example of Scandinavian modernism, the "Annika" bench/coffee table designed by Bruno Mathsson for Karl Mathsson embodies the designer's signature balance of elegance, functionality, and understated craftsmanship. Produced in Sweden during the 1960s, the piece features a long, rectangular top with softly rounded corners, crafted in beautifully grained light oak. Its minimalist silhouette is complemented by slender, gently curved legs that create a sense of lightness while providing excellent stability. Originally conceived as a versatile furnishing, the "Annika" functions equally well as a bench or an elongated coffee table, making it a timeless addition to both contemporary and classic interiors. The clean lines and organic proportions reflect the enduring principles of Scandinavian design, where comfort, utility, and natural materials are seamlessly integrated. The warm oak surface showcases a rich patina developed over decades, enhancing the character of the piece while celebrating the quality of its construction. Elegant yet practical, the "Annika" is a collectible work of mid-century Swedish design, admired for its restrained aesthetic, exceptional craftsmanship, and enduring versatility.

name: Table 'Annika' designed by Bruno Mathsson for Karl Mathsson,
Table in the style of Josef Frank
Bedside table for DUX
description: The colonial-style combination of cane, rattan, and teak makes this Scandinavian bedside table design particularly interesting. The woven edges and metal handles create a striking decorative contrast. Both bedside tables are very sturdy and in good original condition. Initially, the Swedish furniture manufacturer DUX specialised in the production of beds, but later they diversified and famously realised various iconic designs by Bruno Mathsson.

name: Side table designed by Jens Quistgaard
description: Executed in teak, the table features a circular top with a gently recessed centre, functioning as a removable tray. The top is constructed from multiple segments, carefully joined to emphasise the natural variation of the wood grain. It stands on four cylindrical legs, slightly tapered, joined to the underside with a simple and functional construction. The arrangement of the legs provides stability while maintaining a light visual presence. The proportions are compact, making it suitable as a side or occasional table. Jens Quistgaard is best known for his work with Dansk Designs, where he developed a wide range of domestic objects characterised by clarity of form and practicality. This table reflects the same approach, combining straightforward construction with attention to material and detail.

name: Dining table model 752 designed by Josef Frank for Svenskt Tenn
Desk designed by Alvar Andersson for Hyresgästföreningen, retailed by G.A. Berg
description: Gustaf Axel Berg ran his own shop and workshop on Kungsgatan in central Stockholm between 1933 and 1944. His production was mostly on commission for offices in the 1930s and, as functionalism slowly gained recognition, also for private interiors in the late 1930s and 1940s. He was the first retailer to import Alvar Aalto's designs to Sweden. G. A. Berg's name is often associated to Swedish Modern. G. A. Berg is represented in the Stockholm National Museum's permanent collection.

name: Table designed by Alvar Aalto for Artek
description: This table, designed by Alvar Aalto for Artek in the 1970s, reflects Aalto’s hallmark design principles of simplicity and functionality. Constructed from lacquered birch with a durable laminate top, the table embodies the clean lines and natural materials central to Aalto’s modernist philosophy. The bentwood legs are a signature feature of Aalto’s work, showcasing his innovative approach to woodworking and his ability to blend form with practicality. The laminate surface provides durability, making the table as practical as it is aesthetically pleasing. A timeless piece, this table is a testament to Aalto’s enduring influence on modern design, seamlessly integrating into both contemporary and traditional interiors.

name: Side table designed by Severin Hansen Jr.
Table designed by Göran Castell for the school of Carl Malmsten
Library table designed by Uno Åhrén for Svenskt Tenn
description: Uno Åhrén (1897-1977) was a prominent Swedish architect and urban planner, playing a ket role in the development of functionalism in Sweden during the early 20th century. As a central figure in the Swedish modernist movement, Åhrén’s work was rooted in the belief that design should prioritise functionality, simplicity, and the needs of modern living. Åhrén collaborated with Svenskt Tenn in the late 1920s and early 1930s, contributing to the evolution of modern Swedish design. Together with Estrid Ericson, he helped define the principles of Swedish modernism—merging functionality with refined aesthetics—and laid the foundation for Svenskt Tenn’s enduring influence in interior design. His collaboration with Svenskt Tenn was prominently featured at the Stockholm Exhibition of 1930, a pivotal event for Swedish functionalism. Here, Åhrén’s ideas about modern living environments gained widespread recognition, showcasing how design could improve everyday life through thoughtful, rational solutions. Åhrén’s commitment to functionalism is evident in his furniture designs for Svenskt Tenn, characterised by clean lines, geometric clarity, and a restrained aesthetic. This table reflects these principles, highlighting his focus on simplicity, material integrity, and the seamless integration of form and function. Early maker's mark underneath the surface.

name: Side table designed by Severin Hansen Jr. for Haslev Möbelsnedkeri
Table model 70 designed by Alvar Aalto for G. A. Berg
description: The Table, model 70, designed by Alvar Aalto for G. A. Berg in the 1930s, is a prime example of Aalto’s innovative approach to furniture design. Crafted from birch with a lacquered finish, the table combines functional simplicity with the organic beauty of natural materials. Its elegant round top and lower shelf provide both utility and aesthetic charm, while the bentwood legs, a hallmark of Aalto's work, contribute to its clean and modern profile. Alvar Aalto’s collaboration with G. A. Berg, a Swedish furniture manufacturer, was an important chapter in his design career, marking his entry into Scandinavian modernism during the 1930s. Aalto created a range of innovative furniture for G. A. Berg that highlighted his pioneering approach to bentwood techniques, functional simplicity, and a deep respect for natural materials. This partnership also contributed to the spread of Aalto’s designs beyond Finland, as G. A. Berg’s manufacturing capabilities made his work more accessible across Scandinavia and Europe. Pieces from this collaboration, such as Model 70 tables and early bentwood chairs, are now highly collectible, representing the evolution of modern furniture design during a pivotal era for Aalto’s career.

name: Serving trolley model 756 designed by Josef Frank for Svenskt Tenn
description: This serving trolley, model 756, was designed by Josef Frank for Svenskt Tenn during the 1940s. Executed in veneered walnut with brass details, the piece is characterised by its balanced proportions and light construction. The slender legs terminate in brass castors, allowing the trolley to move easily within a room, while the warm tone of the walnut lends the piece a quiet elegance. Designed as a versatile serving or tea trolley, the model features folding drop-leaf sides that allow the surface to expand when needed and fold down when not in use. The design reflects Frank’s interest in furniture that is both adaptable and visually light, suited to everyday living without sacrificing refinement. Josef Frank (1885–1967) was an Austrian-born architect, designer, and artist who later became a Swedish citizen. After relocating to Sweden in the 1930s, he began a long collaboration with Estrid Ericson and her company Svenskt Tenn. There he developed a distinctive design language that combined Viennese elegance with the functional ideals of Scandinavian modernism. His furniture, textiles, and interiors remain among the most celebrated expressions of twentieth-century Swedish design.

name: Table with a pair of benches
Dining table model 1197 designed by Josef Frank for Svenskt Tenn
description: This simple yet elegant dining table is an excellent example of how Josef Frank combined Viennese elegance with Swedish functionalism to achieve a truly unique design style. The mahogany dining table exudes a sense of luxury owing to the naturally rich tones of the wood. The tabletop can be extended by raising the two drop leaf ends that are attached by discreet hinges. These drop leaf extensions are held in place by supporting struts that pull out from the underside of the table’s surface. An expertly crafted shaker-style base supports the tabletop. Shaker furniture was developed by a religious group that valued simplicity and utility. These beliefs were reflected in the functional form of minimalist design. Together with Estrid Ericson and her furnishing company, Svenskt Tenn, Josef Frank sought to incorporate natural forms and colours into his interiors. His aim was to give the inhabitants a sense of freedom in enclosed spaces. Josef Frank believed that “ornament and complexity create peacefulness and get rid of the disturbing aspect of pure functional form”. Josef Frank’s impact on Swedish design is unparalleled.

name: Occasional table model 2168 designed by Josef Frank for Svenskt Tenn
description: Josef Frank’s occasional table model 2168 is one of his rarer models. Its beautifully carved, turned legs give it a lighter and more playful aesthetic. The black granite top provides a considerable contrast to the walnut frame. Simplicity and exceptional quality make this piece a timeless Svenskt Tenn collectible.

name: Sideboard designed by Axel Einar Hjorth
Occasional table
Occasional table for Oy Stockmann AB
description: The most compelling aspect of this occasional table is the relationship of its legs to the surface. With splayed tapering legs, the well thought out design resembles an animal — its four obtuse angles bring to mind an antelope bending down to drink water. This piece was made for Stockmann in Helsinki, Finland's most exclusive department store. Since the legs extend far out to each side, the table is very stable with extra frame support under the surface. The richness of the elm wood's colour is beautiful.

name: Dining table designed by Knud Jörgensen
description: This mid-century Danish dining table is of the highest quality, with cross-section stretchers overlapping underneath the table’s surface. The table is sculptural yet composed of solid wood, making it very stable. Honduran Mahogany is one of the most exclusive woods used in furniture making; its colour and grain structure are remarkable. Side aprons connect the table’s curved surface and solid legs for additional balance, adding another expensive detail to the design. The size and quality of workmanship indicate that Knud Jörgensen, an incredibly skilled cabinetmaker, probably made this piece a special order.

name: Dining table designed by Kaare Klint for Rud. Rasmussen
description: This model is one of the rarest and finest dining tables by the Danish master Kaare Klint. Carefully chosen woodgrain textures frame each part of the table's mahogany surface. The elegant table has an efficient extension mechanism; Klint implemented the "Dutch pull-out" system that allows for practical leaf storage underneath the table's surface. The leaf extensions are cleverly built into the frame and can be pulled out from each end when needed. With its exquisite woodwork and carved details on all four legs, this table perfectly matches Klint's "Red Chairs". The table is in excellent condition with only minor signs of use, which is astonishing considering its age. A private Swedish collector previously owned it. Kaare Klint was the father of Scandinavian modernism and is responsible for bringing Danish design to the centre stage. History has rarely seen such an impact left on the world of design by just one person, as Kaare Klint created a design language that would be spoken by designers for decades to come. The Danish golden age and Scandinavian modernism are periods that made Kaare Klint’s name synonymous with icon. Kaare Klint’s appreciation for clean lines, simple ornamentation and an understanding of the human body translated into a design philosophy that has truly influenced the designs of today. Kaare Klint crafted pieces that embodied a perfect balance of form and function. This balance was achieved from his education as an apprentice in his father’s architectural practice. This is where he was educated in classic realism and ergonomics, this allowed him to understand the proportions and requirements of furniture. Kaare Klint’s training focused a great deal on classical design on a global scale. Egyptian neoclassical design elements run through the veins of pieces. The pieces Kaare Klint crafted encapsulate technical perfection, masked by a minimalist aesthetic. The joinery flawlessly fits together, questioning whether the pieces were crafted from a single block of wood. Kaare Klint’s legacy was imbued in the physical, his architectural and furniture masterpieces and the philosophical, as a lecturer Kaare Klint passed on his knowledge to students that would continue to inspire pieces based on his design philosophy. Marked.

name: Occasional table designed by Thomas Sandell, for Asplund
description: The significance of this piece lies in its contrasts. Initially designed for the company Asplund, the table has a solid birch top with a built-in fruit bowl on a green lacquered base. While the convex outside of the bowl is composed of blocks to create a pyramid effect, the inside is entirely flat and smooth, creating a very intriguing design variation. The lower part of the table looks industrial with its welded metal base, and yet it shows such unique wooden handicraft on top. This particular table might be the only one ever made and comes from the designer's private collection. Asplund frequently commissioned designers to create exciting pieces that never went into production; this table proved very expensive to produce since creating a table with an inbuilt wooden bowl was and still is extremely difficult.

name: Dining table designed by Börge Mogensen for Söborg
description: Strong constructions, simple lines, and natural materials characterize the aesthetic of Börge Mogensen, one of Denmark’s most influential mid-century designers. This model, known as the “Hunting Table”, is one of Börge Mogensen’s classics. He designed these robust, functional tables for country houses and everyday use. The brass stretchers are typical features used by Mogensen for extra stability and visual contrast.

name: Occasional table designed by Frits Schlegel
description: The intriguing combination of rosewood and patinated brass is emphasised by the shape of this large occasional table from 1949. The offset slats that make up the round shelf under the table’s surface create a diagonal pattern, which lightens the overall design. The angled, somewhat industrial-looking legs echo the shape of the matching armchairs’ front legs. Together they become a noteworthy set of Scandinavian design collectables. This distinctly modern set was designed by Frits Schlegel for the resistance fighter Erik Nyegaard’s villa on Strandvejen in Copenhagen, a very exclusive road close to the seaside. Frits Schlegel trained as a mason and studied to become an architect at the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts. Frits Schlegel’s oeuvre holds different projects; his furniture designs stand out as works of remarkable craftsmanship with a modern aesthetic. Unique.

name: Dining table designed by Hans J. Wegner for Andreas Tuck
Occasional table designed by Frits Henningsen
Occasional table / Bench model 5273, designed by Börge Mogensen for Fredericia Stolefabrik
Occasional table 'Rhythmic Plywood' model 9015 designed by Tapio Wirkkala for Asko
description: The Rhythmic Plywood table, designed by Tapio Wirkkala in 1957 for Asko, is a distinctive example of Finnish post-war design. The rectangular tabletop is crafted from maple and birch and features three oval inlays that reveal the layered structure of laminated plywood. These patterns are created by cutting through a block of laminated wood, exposing the rhythmic lines of the layers and forming decorative shapes reminiscent of natural growth rings. The tabletop rests on slender steel legs finished with small brass feet, creating a light and elegant contrast to the warm surface of the wood. This combination of refined metal elements with expressive plywood detailing reflects Wirkkala’s ability to merge craftsmanship with modern industrial techniques. Tapio Wirkkala (1915–1985) was one of the most influential figures in Finnish post-war design. Trained at the Central School of Applied Arts in Helsinki, he worked across a wide range of disciplines including glass, furniture, graphics, and sculpture. Deeply inspired by the forms and textures of nature, Wirkkala frequently incorporated organic patterns into his work, particularly through innovative uses of laminated plywood and carved surfaces. Stamped.

name: Occasional table / Bench model 5274, designed by Börge Mogensen for Fredericia Stolefabrik
description: This iconic design by Børge Mogensen, model 5274, was created for Fredericia Stolefabrik and remains a defining example of mid-century Danish modernism. The versatile piece is crafted with a solid oak frame and features a woven rattan top, often referred to as star weave or star rattan, which adds a distinctive texture to the piece. Its thoughtful dimensions allow it to serve as both a coffee table and a bench, showcasing Mogensen’s ability to merge practicality with style. This design reflects the mid-century trend for multifunctional, space-saving furniture, which could easily adapt to a range of domestic needs. Fredericia Stolefabrik, established in 1911, played an integral role in the production of Danish modern furniture, collaborating with some of the country’s most renowned designers to create timeless pieces that emphasize quality and craftsmanship. Børge Mogensen (1914–1972) was a key figure in Danish furniture design. A graduate of the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts in Copenhagen, Mogensen was influenced by Kaare Klint's human-centered approach to design. Known for his pragmatic and functional designs, Mogensen’s work has become synonymous with the ideals of Danish modernism, focusing on simplicity, comfort, and craftsmanship. Marked.

name: Side table
description: Rosewood with metal frame and legs.

name: Bedside table model 914 designed by Josef Frank for Svenskt Tenn
description: Model 914 is an elegant bedside table designed by Josef Frank in the 1950s for Svenskt Tenn. Crafted in mahogany, the piece is defined by its balanced proportions and understated detailing. A rectangular top with slightly raised edges sits above a single drawer fitted with a curved brass handle. The design demonstrates Frank’s characteristic approach to furniture: clear structure, thoughtful functionality, and the use of refined materials. Its restrained form allows the table to integrate easily into a wide range of interiors, whether paired with modern furnishings or more traditional settings. The combination of warm mahogany and polished brass adds a quiet sense of elegance while maintaining the simplicity that defines much of Frank’s work. Josef Frank (1885–1967) was an Austrian-born architect, designer, and artist who later became a Swedish citizen. After moving to Sweden in the 1930s, he began a long collaboration with Estrid Ericson and her company Svenskt Tenn, where he developed a distinctive design language. His furniture, textiles, and interiors remain among the most influential contributions to mid-century Swedish design.

name: Desk 'AT 305' designed by Hans J. Wegner for Andreas Tuck
description: Stamped.

name: Side table designed by Anti Hakkarainen for Taidetakomo Hakkarainen
description: This side table, designed by Anti Hakkarainen in 1949 and produced by his workshop Taidetakomo Hakkarainen, combines expressive ironwork with a richly detailed mosaic surface. The wrought iron base is composed of slender legs shaped into rope-like twists, a technique closely associated with Hakkarainen’s metalwork. The tabletop is framed by a pierced iron gallery and set with a colourful stone mosaic. The scene depicts a stylised outdoor setting with two figures standing beside a long-necked bird, possibly a heron or crane, framed by slender trees and geometric landscape elements. The composition is assembled from small pieces of coloured stone and marble, arranged in a painterly manner that contrasts with the dark iron structure. Anti Hakkarainen emerged as an important figure in Finnish decorative arts during the 1930s. Educated at the School of Applied Arts in Helsinki, he later established his atelier Taidetakomo A. Hakkarainen, where he developed a distinctive approach to wrought iron furniture and decorative objects. His work often merges modernist clarity with subtle Art Deco influences and exceptional craftsmanship. In recognition of his contribution to Nordic design, one of his tables was acquired by the Nationalmuseum in Stockholm in 2015. Marked.

name: Occasional table 'Tulip' designed by Eero Saarinen for Knoll International
description: The Tulip table, designed by Eero Saarinen in the mid-1950s for Knoll, is one of the most recognisable pieces of twentieth-century modern furniture. The design pairs a circular Carrara marble top with a single pedestal base, creating a clear and elegant silhouette. The sculptural column rises from a wide, gently flared foot and supports the tabletop in a continuous, flowing form. Saarinen developed the design in response to what he described as the visual clutter created by traditional four-legged tables and chairs. By reducing the structure to a single central support, he sought to eliminate what he called the “slum of legs” beneath the table, producing a cleaner and more harmonious arrangement in the interior. The table forms part of Saarinen’s Pedestal Collection for Knoll, introduced in the late 1950s and including dining tables, side tables, and the well-known Tulip chair. Each piece follows the same single-stem principle, combining industrial materials with organic form. Eero Saarinen (1910–1961) was a Finnish-American architect and designer whose work helped define mid-century modern design. Known for both his architecture and furniture, he collaborated closely with Knoll to produce several iconic pieces. His designs are distinguished by their sculptural clarity and their ability to merge modern technology with expressive, organic form. Marked.

name: Occasional table Annika designed by Bruno Mathsson for Karl Mathsson
description: The Annika occasional table, designed by Bruno Mathsson in the 1930s, is a refined example of early Scandinavian Modern design, reflecting principles of lightness, balance, and structural clarity. Later produced by Karl Mathsson, the model represents Mathsson’s early exploration of functional and ergonomic furniture through innovative construction techniques and careful attention to proportion. The design features a round tabletop supported by a three-legged base composed of bentwood elements. These steam-bent wooden components create a delicate yet stable tripod structure, giving the table its distinctive sense of visual lightness. The contrast between the circular tabletop and the sculptural three-legged base demonstrates Mathsson’s interest in combining simplicity with technical innovation. Designed as a versatile occasional table, the Annika can be placed beside seating or used as a small coffee table. Its construction reflects Mathsson’s design philosophy, which emphasized ergonomic function, honest materials, and minimal ornamentation. Today, the Annika remains valued as an important example of early Scandinavian modernism, recognised for its clarity of form, craftsmanship, and timeless proportions. Stamped.

name: Table 'Annika' designed by Bruno Mathsson for Karl Mathsson
Bench / Table designed by Sigvard Nilsson for Söwe-Konst
Occasional table designed by Ib Kofod-Larsen for Christensen & Larsen
Occasional table PK61 designed by Poul Kjaerholm for E. Kold Christensen
description: The PK61 table, designed by Poul Kjærholm in 1956, is a clear expression of the designer’s philosophy of structural clarity and material honesty. The table consists of four identical brushed steel elements that support a square marble top, forming a composition in which every part of the construction is visible. Rather than concealing joints or structure, the design celebrates the relationship between the metal frame and the stone surface. The tabletop is made from Porsgrunn marble, notable for its natural fossil inclusions and subtle variation in tone. Poul Kjærholm (1929–1980) was one of Denmark’s most influential modern furniture designers. Originally trained as a cabinetmaker, he later studied at the Danish School of Arts and Crafts in Copenhagen, where he developed a distinctive approach to furniture design centred on structural clarity and material integrity. Kjærholm frequently combined steel with natural materials such as leather, wood, marble and cane, producing designs that remain celebrated for their precision and timeless simplicity. In 1955 he began a long collaboration with manufacturer E. Kold Christensen, a partnership that continued throughout his career and played a key role in bringing his most iconic designs to production. Stamped.

name: Occasional table model 974 'Tea table' designed by Josef Frank for Svenskt Tenn,
Side / Bedside table
Side table designed by Carl Axel Acking for Svenska Möbelfabrikerna Bodafors
Set of five tables designed by Palle Suenson for J. C. A. Jensen
description: Palle Suenson (1904–1987) was one of Denmark's great, Modernist architects in the 20th century. His work covers a wide range, from single-family townhouses to large-scale office buildings and public institutions. In 1938 young Suenson was commissioned to design a new office building for Aarhus Oil Factory A/S which resulted in a Functionalist building covered in 5,500 custom-made ceramic tiles. The commission also included interior, furniture and lighting, most of which were custom-made for the project. The office floors were constructed with the flexibility of movable walls to be able to quickly accommodate the changing needs, and the present addition tables embrace this purpose naturally. Suenson very carefully created interiors that would age gracefully, which these tables embody with their timeless design, solid wood and elegant details. The building was completed and inaugurated in 1942.

name: Coffee table designed by Frode Holm for Illums Bolighus
Coffee table designed by Arne Jacobsen for Fritz Hansen
description: Rare bronze version.

name: Occasional table designed by Josef Frank for Svenskt Tenn
Desk / Dining table, anonymous
Occasional table designed by Mogens Lassen for T. Madsen
description: This occasional table was designed by Mogens Lassen for the Danish cabinetmaker T. Madsen in 1953. The rectangular structure is supported by four slender, square-section legs. The upper section is enclosed on all sides by woven cane panels set within a dark wooden frame. The cane creates a clear contrast with the darker timber and gives the table a lighter visual character. The legs terminate in darker sections, adding a restrained decorative detail. The construction is simple and carefully proportioned, with straight lines and a clearly defined geometric structure. The table reflects Mogens Lassen’s architectural approach to furniture design, with an emphasis on function, proportion and structural clarity. The use of cane around the full perimeter distinguishes the design and is characteristic of Danish furniture production of the period, where traditional materials were combined with precise modern forms.

name: Wall hung table designed by Helge Vestergaard Jensen, for Peder Pedersen
